This is basic first-aid guidance for demonstration purposes only. It does not replace professional medical training or emergency services.
Severe Bleeding Control
Call for emergency help immediately, or have someone else call.
Apply firm, direct pressure on the wound using a clean cloth or bandage.
If the cloth soaks through, do not remove it — add more layers on top and keep pressing.
Keep the injured area raised above heart level if possible.
Keep the person still, warm, and calm while waiting for help.
Do not apply a tourniquet unless trained and bleeding cannot be controlled by pressure.
Fractures & Immobilization
Do not try to straighten or push the limb back into place.
Keep the injured area as still as possible.
If available, support the limb above and below the injury with a splint (a rolled towel, magazine, or board).
Pad around the splint before securing it loosely — never tie it tight enough to cut off circulation.
Check fingers or toes for color and warmth after splinting.
Get the person to professional medical care as soon as possible.
Burns
Move the person away from the source of the burn.
Cool the burn under cool (not ice-cold) running water for at least 10–20 minutes.
Remove tight clothing or jewelry near the burn before it swells, but do not remove anything stuck to the skin.
Cover loosely with a clean, non-fluffy cloth or cling film — do not apply ice, butter, or ointments.
Do not pop any blisters.
Seek medical help for burns larger than the palm, on the face/hands/joints, or if the skin looks white or charred.
Shock
Call for emergency help immediately.
Lay the person down and raise their legs about 12 inches, unless a leg or spine injury is suspected.
Keep them warm with a blanket or coat.
Loosen tight clothing around the neck, chest, and waist.
Do not give them anything to eat or drink.
Keep talking calmly to them and monitor breathing until help arrives.
Choking
Ask \"Are you choking?\" — if they can cough or speak, encourage them to keep coughing.
If they cannot breathe, speak, or cough, stand behind them and give up to 5 sharp back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand.
If back blows don\'t clear it, give up to 5 abdominal thrusts: stand behind them, fist above the navel, pull sharply inward and upward.
Alternate 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts until the object clears or they become unresponsive.
If the person becomes unresponsive, lower them to the ground, call emergency services immediately, and begin CPR guidance.
Positioning (Recovery Position)
If the person is unconscious but breathing normally, place them in the recovery position on their side.
Tilt their head back slightly to keep the airway open.
Bend the top leg at the knee to stabilize the body.
Keep monitoring their breathing continuously until help arrives.
If breathing stops at any point, begin CPR guidance immediately.
CPR Overview
Check responsiveness — tap and shout. If unresponsive and not breathing normally, call emergency services immediately.
Place the person on their back on a firm, flat surface.
Kneel beside them, place the heel of one hand on the center of the chest, other hand on top, fingers interlocked.
Push hard and fast — about 5–6 cm deep, at a rate of 100–120 compressions per minute — letting the chest fully rise between compressions.
Continue compressions until emergency help arrives or the person starts breathing normally. Only add rescue breaths if trained to do so.
This is a basic overview only — professional CPR/first-aid training is strongly recommended.
